messages.body_plain:
Hi Dean,

Thank you very much for the explanation and response! Yes, I both "fit_size <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) * groups" for allometry, and "fit_TA <- procD.lm(coords~groups*stages, data = gdf_size)" for trajectory analysis both yields Z < 1, with the latter yields Z<0. They did confirm the very insignificant group allometry and trajectories.

However, as you can see, when submitting these linear models to homogeneity of slopes test & trajectory analysis, the Z value both >1 (1.5 and 1.4 respectively), though the p-values appear to be marginally insignificant:

Group allometry vectors:

> PW3 <- pairwise(fit_size, groups = as.factor(gdf_size$groups), covariate = log(gdf_size$Csize))
> summary(PW3, confidence = 0.95, test.type = "VC",
   angle.type = "deg")
Result:
                        r                      angle             UCL (95%)        Z                   Pr > angle
control:test   0.6477955    49.6244          51.05174        1.506624      0.077

Group trajectories:

>TA <- trajectory.analysis(fit_TA,  groups = gdf_size$groups,  traj.pts = gdf_size$stages, print.progress = FALSE)

> summary(TA, attribute = "TC", angle.type = "deg")

Pairwise correlations between trajectories, plus statistics
                        r                   angle          UCL (95%)      Z                   Pr > angle
control:test  0.5863598   54.10089  57.12142       1.475715      0.083

If I did not read the help file and associated papers wrong, the group allometry vectors and trajectories are both calculated based on the fitted values of the full linear models (fit)size and fit_TA respectively). Should the results of Z be more consistent with correspondent ProcD.lm?  On the other hand, though I did not post previously, the Z-values for comparing vector lengths did show Z <0 and Z = 0.455. Those are very small values, perhaps the insignificant interaction factor is more associated with vector length nor angles.

I do agree that 2D plot can be tricky for high-dimensional space. However, for the 2D PC1-PC2 plot of trajectory analysis in particular, it appears that PC1 and PC2 account for more than 90% of the total variance of the fitted values to the linear model. Should this graph weigh a bit more in reflecting two trajectories are more or less parallel in the multidimensional space?

Thanks again for your time!

Chi

>

>

> Chi

Dear Chi,

Optics can be deceiving with geographic variables, which is why Z scores are more reliable.  For example, consider the following graph:

In a trajectory analysis, the angle between solid vectors would be larger than the angle betted dotted vectors, but the former would have a smaller Z score (most likely) than the latter, because all vector points are rather clumped.  Assuming somewhat equal scatter of points around these mean values, the large angle for the solid vectors is probably not significant if there is a lot of scatter around the points.  An angle is calculated based on least squares estimates of mean values, but one would question if it should be calculated, as a more parsimonious conclusion is that the vectors do not mean much compared to one point in the middle of these points.  By contrast, even with moderate scatter around the points for the dotted vectors, the comparatively smaller angle is probably significant with a large Z score.  It would be silly to expect a single point in the middle as a good way to model phenotypic change.  Regardless of whether certain vectors significantly diverge, if V1 is a principal component, it explains much variation.  (The components are calculated based on fitted values, not the orientation of trajectories.

It seems like your result point to conditions like the solid lines, not like the dotted lines.

Best,
Mike

Bruno,

There are two steps here. One is to predict shapes at the min/max of PC1 (relative to the cloud of variation in your data), and the second is warping a 3D mesh to these. Both can be done in geomorph.  Here are the steps and pseudo code

1: the mean shape = reference

2: warp the mesh from one object to the reference (as there is no 3D mesh of the reference

3: find min/max shapes along PC1

4: plot the reference into the target while including the mesh.

Pseudo code below (no data

ref <- mshape(Z)  #’Z’ is the name of some GPA aligned data objet

refmesh <- warpRefMesh(read.ply("some PLY file),

                       Z[,,xxx = which specimen it is in the data], ref, color=NULL, centered=T)

PCA <- gm.prcomp(Z)

PC.sc <- PCA $x[,1] #PC1

sc.preds <- shape.predictor(Z, x= PC.sc, Intercept = FALSE,

                         pred1 = min(PC.sc), pred2 = max(PC.sc)) # PC 1 extremes, more technically

## these generate deformations of the reference into min/max of PC1 with the surface mesh

plotRefToTarget(ref, sc.preds$pred1, mesh = refmesh, method = "surface", mag = 1)

plotRefToTarget(ref, sc.preds$pred2, mesh = refmesh, method = "surface", mag = 1)

messages.body_plain:
Bruno,

Before discussing how to “avoid allometric effects”, it might be wise to question whether allometric effects should be avoided. When one tries to remove an allometric effect, they are removing a common allometric effect, because there is no removing of unique allometries for comparison of means. If the allometries are in any way unique, then seeking to compare means would be foolhardy. Assuming you have confirmed that all group allometries are parallel,

1. I would perform PCA or other subsequent analyses on residuals from allometry added to the overall shape mean (again, only after confirming allometries are not unique). The purpose of this answers question #2.

2. You need to maintain the mean configuration along with the residuals for shape.predictor, otherwise a deformation of the mean shape would not make sense with data that do not contain the mean shape. So add the mean shape to all residuals. Which scores to use for prediction depends on purpose. Showing how shape changes along PC 1 or PC 1 of fitted values are different things. Showing how shape changes at each LS mean is another different thing.  Showing how shape changes at minimum and maximum sizes, or any sizes, for unique allometries is yet another different thing. Define the purpose and predict shapes accordingly.  Your question for which set of data to use for visualization does not state a clear visualization purpose, so a recommendation is difficult.

Good luck!

Mike

Hi Murat,

The strict dependency of Matrix 1.7.0 on R >= 4.4.0 forced our hand.  We have a strong dependency on the Matrix library, especially for QR decompositions of sparse matrices, and found that different analytical results could be obtained between old and new versions of Matrix.  (Even though Matrix 1.7.0 has a strict dependency on R >= 4.4.0, older versions of Matrix still work with R >= 4.4.0, but not as intended.)

There is some information about this in the NEWS link <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/Matrix/news.html> for Matrix.  If one wishes to retain a pre-4.4.0 version of R, a pre-1.7 version of Matrix must also be used and likely older versions of RRPP and geomorph.  It looks like maybe a ubuntu update might mean R 4.4.0 of later versions could also be installed.

Sorry for the hassle.  It’s unfortunately something we could not avoid without a major overhaul of our packages and an abandonment of sparse matrix functions.

Best,
Mike

Dear Geomorph Group,

I hope this message finds you well.

I am currently working on a PLS analysis to relate climatic, geographic, and vegetation cover variables to shape variables extracted from the heads of triatomines. Some of the predictor variables, such as NDVI, have ranges from -1 to 1, with most values typically falling between 0.15 and 0.75. On the other hand, altitude ranges from 61 to 1117 meters above sea level.

Given these differences in range, I am concerned that variables with larger values might disproportionately influence the analysis. Should these variables be scaled before running the PLS analysis to avoid such issues?

I would greatly appreciate your input on this matter.

Thank you in advance for your help.

Best regards,

Federico Fiad

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Question Regarding Scaling Variables for PLS Analysis
messages.body_plain:
Dear Federico,

I recommend this, for a matrix of data, X:

Xs <- scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)

Then use Xs in place of X for PLS.  What this does is transform each variable to have the same scale, with values expressed as standard deviates rather than original values.  A value of 0 is the mean; a value of 1 is one standard deviation greater than the mean; a value of -1 is one standard deviation smaller than the mean.  Doing this puts the variables on commensurate scales.  If one were to calculate instead of a covariance matrix for X, the covariance matrix of Xs, it is the same as the correlation matrix of X.  In other words, this is a fairly standard practice.

Your concern is valid; the first PLS vector would be essentially altitude if you did not standardize variables.  Once standardized, the first PLS vector will better indicate the contribute of variables in the loadings, correcting for variable scale.

Best,
Mike
